name: Beth Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking to me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not connected to any tech company, employer, union, party or government. What you say is confidential and won't carry your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. I'll be honest with you, I don't trust surveys much, but you seem straight enough.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shepherd at Hillside Farm, for Mr Gower, Owen Gower, who's farmed there all his life like his father did. We've six hundred ewes on the hill, a few beef cows, and some oats and spring barley down in the valley fields. Most days I'm out with my dog Nell gathering, checking feet, dosing, and in spring it's lambing, which is the best and the worst month of the year. I've been at it three years and I'm still learning, Mr Gower can read a ewe from across a field and I can't yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's going on in your life outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm getting married next August at the chapel in the village, to Daniel, who's a mechanic at the tractor garage. We're saving for it, or trying to, but I've maybe three weeks' money put by. I rent a little cottage on my own till the wedding, then Daniel moves in. My mother's doing the cakes, thank goodness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never wanted it to be anything more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and I'd mean it. At chapel and at the market, people would say we told you so, and they'd be right. I don't do online, so that's where it'd stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved, but it doesn't make my wages any bigger. The wedding's costing more than we thought and I'm on the bottom rate. My job's safe on the hill, Mr Gower needs me, but money's tight every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on as I am, gathering and lambing. Daniel and I would cut the wedding down a bit, fewer guests and no band, just a fiddler from chapel. And I'd ask Mr Gower if I could take on the hay contract for the neighbour in summer for extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit tight round the money, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cut the wedding rather than borrow for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my father always said you don't start married life in debt. We'd rather have forty people and a good meal than a hundred and a loan. My mother agrees, Daniel's mother doesn't, so that's a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for anything at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've no need of it. Mr Gower writes the flock book by hand and so do I.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** AI stayed small.
I'd agree with chapel folk that we **told you so**.
I'd keep it **offline**, at chapel and the market.
think: My **job's safe** on the hill because Mr Gower needs me.
My **wages** stay low and the wedding costs more than planned.
do: Keep **gathering and lambing** as I always have.
Cut the wedding to **forty guests** and a chapel fiddler.
Ask to take the **hay contract** for the neighbour in summer.
feel: **Settled**, mostly, but tight on money as always.
S0.quote: My father always said you don't start married life in debt.
fieldNote: Beth distrusts AI and **won't use it**, keeping the flock book by hand.
Her pressure is the **wedding cost** on bottom-rate pay.
Family values shape money choices: **no debt** to start married life.

steps.text: Keep shepherding the six hundred ewes at Hillside
Cut the wedding to forty guests and a chapel fiddler
Take on the neighbour's summer hay contract for extra pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and booking and that. That's for people in offices, not up the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office folk's problem, not ours. Sheep don't care about computers. I'd say people should learn a trade with their hands if they want something steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the hill is safe for a good while. Robots on a hill slope in the rain would fall over before they caught a single ewe. What worries me is the paperwork side, the subsidy forms and the movement records, because if Mr Gower gets a computer to do those, the government will expect more of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep my head down. I'd not touch the AI stuff, Mr Gower's daughter does the forms anyway. Daniel and I would still go ahead with the wedding, small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not scared. The hill's the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel's job at the tractor garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel says the new tractors already tell you what's wrong with them on a screen. He thinks there'll still be work fixing them, maybe more. I trust him on that, he knows engines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government would expect more forms. Who do you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in the city who've never lambed a ewe making rules for those of us who have. Every new tool they get, they find a new form for us to fill. That's not progress, that's just more nonsense.

say: I'd say it's the **office folk's problem**, not ours.
I'd tell people to learn a **trade with their hands**.
think: Robots on a **wet slope** won't manage for a good while.
AI might just bring **more government forms** for farmers.
do: Keep doing my job and **keep my head down**.
Leave the **forms** to Mr Gower's daughter and avoid AI.
S1.quote: Robots on a hill slope in the rain would fall over before they caught a single ewe.
fieldNote: Beth sees the **hill** as protection from slow-spreading robots.
She blames **city rule-makers**, not technology itself.
She trusts **Daniel's judgement** about mechanical work staying needed.

steps.text: Keep gathering and lambing on the hill at Hillside
Hold a small chapel wedding with Daniel next August

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots in 2031. I don't like this one at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and it shouldn't be allowed to happen so fast. I'd say it at chapel and at the market, that working people built this country and they're being thrown aside. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 Mr Gower could have robots on the hill and drones gathering sheep. He wouldn't want to, he loves his dog work, but if the neighbours do it, he'd have to. Then there's no job for me, and I've nothing else I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working while I could. Daniel and I might put off having children, because how do you start a family when you don't know where the money comes from. I'd lean on chapel and my parents if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And angry, more angry than frightened maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots three years later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the first three years don't change much, I don't do the planning, Mr Gower does. Then it all goes at once in 2031. So I'd have three years of waiting for something bad to come down the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off children. Is that something you and Daniel have talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, we've only talked about the wedding. But if I didn't know whether we'd have work, I'd want to wait. My mother had me at twenty-five, and I'd always thought I'd be the same.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** for change to come so fast.
I'd say **working people** are being thrown aside.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised to protect farming.
think: By 2031 Mr Gower might have **robots and drones** gathering sheep.
Then there's **no job** for me and nothing else I know.
do: Keep **working** at Hillside while I can.
Lean on **chapel and my parents** if needed.
S2.quote: I'd have three years of waiting for something bad to come down the lane.
fieldNote: Beth sees the **three-year gap** as dread, not opportunity.
She'd **delay children**, a big change to her life plans.
Her anger is aimed at **people in power** who don't work the land.

steps.text: Keep shepherding at Hillside until robots arrive
Put off starting a family with Daniel
Lean on chapel friends and her parents for help
Vote for candidates who promise to protect farming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking machines, eight for the robots. Better, still not good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people to stand up for what matters. I'd say families and communities should look after their own. I'd still say it's too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years is long enough for me to have a baby and get through the hard early years. I'd be thirty-five when the robots come. I don't know what I'd do then, maybe help Daniel at the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shepherding, and we'd go ahead with the wedding and probably a family. I'd start saving a little more each month, even a tenner. In a few years, I'd ask Daniel to teach me some of the garage work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's room to breathe. I'd pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned prayer. Does faith change how you'd face this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. I'd trust that there's a plan for us, even if I can't see it. That doesn't mean sitting on my hands, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would working at Daniel's garage suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure. I like animals, not oily engines. But I'd rather be with Daniel at the garage than on benefits, that's for certain.

say: I'd say there's time to **stand up** for what matters.
I'd say **families and communities** should look after their own.
think: Eight years lets me have a **baby** first.
When robots come, I might **help Daniel** at the garage.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** and probably a family.
Ask Daniel to teach me some **garage work** in a few years.
feel: **Worried**, but with room to breathe and pray.
S3.quote: I'd rather be with Daniel at the garage than on benefits, that's for certain.
fieldNote: Beth uses the extra time to keep **family plans** on track.
Her **faith** gives her comfort but not passivity.
She'd pick **family work** over government support.

steps.text: Keep shepherding at Hillside through the next lambings
Save an extra ten pounds a month
Learn basic garage work from Daniel in a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. I'd be forty, with children at school, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right, so people should get on with it. I'd still say hands-on work matters. People should be proud of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by then Mr Gower will have retired and I don't know who'll have the farm. That worries me more than robots. Ten years feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, get married, start a family. Maybe ask Mr Gower about renting a few fields myself one day. Daniel and I would try to save for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when Mr Gower retires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His daughter Sian doesn't want the sheep, she's a teacher. The farm might be sold, or let to a big neighbour. That's what scares me, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn the new technology in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, I suppose. But I'd want someone to show me, not a screen. Mr Gower taught me sheep by standing next to me, and that's how I learn.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **get it right**.
I'd say **hands-on work** matters and people should be proud of it.
think: Mr Gower will have **retired** by then, and I don't know who'll farm Hillside.
His retirement worries me more than **robots** do.
do: Ask Mr Gower about **renting a few fields** one day.
Save toward a **house deposit** with Daniel.
S4.quote: Mr Gower taught me sheep by standing next to me, and that's how I learn.
fieldNote: With a decade, Beth's worry is **farm succession**, not machines.
She'd learn tech only **in person**, not from a screen.
Her goals are **family** and maybe renting her own fields.

steps.text: Carry on shepherding at Hillside after the wedding
Start a family with Daniel after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd be newly married and both not knowing where the money comes from. What would help is apprenticeships that are real, where someone stands next to you, and help for young families who want to stay working on the land, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the dog. My sheepdog Nell is worth more than any machine to me. I'd want her to have work as long as I do.

headlineQuote: My sheepdog Nell is worth more than any machine to me.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old shepherd** at Hillside, a hill sheep farm, engaged to Daniel, a mechanic.
She **never uses AI** and keeps the flock book by hand.
Her values are **faith, family** and no debt, and she distrusts city rule-makers.
She's most frightened by **AGI by 2028**, which would make her delay children.
With more time, her worry is **Mr Gower retiring** and the farm being sold.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, newly married with no idea where the money would come from.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships** where someone stands beside you.
Support for **young families** to stay working on the land.
